blocks.text: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use; define narrow interfaces per client role.

A fat interface couples every client to every method: a change to `fax` recompiles and retests print-only code, and implementers must stub operations they cannot support. Split by **role** as the client sees it, then let one class implement several **role interfaces** when it really does several things.

items: **Cut line:** what a client calls, not what an implementer offers.
**Symptoms:** stubs that throw, mocks with fifteen stubbed methods, unrelated imports.
**Result:** small interfaces, often one method, that lambdas can implement.

blocks.text: ISP is LSP's preventive medicine: a narrow interface leaves nothing for an implementer to fake.

cards.expectedOutput:
before: scan() unsupported
basic: [Q3 report]
print Q3 report
lambda Q3 report
fax memo to 555-0100

walkthrough.note: One `Machine` interface bundles three capabilities. A printer-only device must implement `scan` and `fax` by throwing.
Role interfaces, cut by what a client calls. Each has one method, so each is also a valid lambda target.
Implementers choose the roles they really support. `BasicPrinter` is only a `Printer`; `OfficeMachine` is all three.
`ReportJob` asks only for `Printer`. It runs against a basic printer, an office machine or a lambda, and can never call `fax`.

blocks.text: One user-store interface serving a dashboard and a batch importer.

A `UserStore` interface had fourteen methods. The read-only dashboard depended on all of them, so tests mocked writes it never made, and a read replica could not implement the interface at all. It was split into `UserReader` and `UserWriter`. The primary store implements both, the replica only the reader, and the dashboard is wired to `UserReader`.

lines: final class PgStore implements UserReader, UserWriter { ... }

blocks.text: Payoff: the dashboard cannot write, replicas fit the type system, and mocks shrink to two methods.

lists.title: Use when
items: An implementer must throw or no-op for some inherited methods.
Clients use disjoint subsets of one interface.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Roles always change and are used together: splitting adds names, not decoupling.
Every client calls every method: there is nothing to segregate.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Interface-per-method with no role meaning, such as `Doer` or `Getter`.
A client needing five role interfaces often signals an SRP problem.
Intersection bounds like `<T extends A & B>` spreading through APIs.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Functional interfaces are ISP at its limit: one method, any lambda.
`default` methods evolve an interface without breaking implementers, but do not shrink what clients see.

rows.difference: SRP shapes classes by reasons to change; ISP shapes interfaces by what each client calls.
Narrow interfaces leave no method an implementer must fake, which keeps subtypes substitutable.
When a fat third-party interface cannot be split, adapt it to the narrow role your client needs.
A facade simplifies a subsystem for callers by hiding it; ISP narrows an existing interface to a client's needs.

entries.name: java.util.function
entries.detail: `Supplier`, `Function`, `Predicate` and friends are one-method role interfaces.

entries.name: ReadableByteChannel, WritableByteChannel, ByteChannel
entries.detail: `java.nio.channels` separates read and write roles; `ByteChannel` combines them.

entries.name: java.io.Closeable and Flushable
entries.detail: Independent capabilities that a class can add separately, rather than one stream mega-interface.

entries.name: CrudRepository, ListCrudRepository, PagingAndSortingRepository
entries.detail: Repository capabilities are separate interfaces that you extend selectively.

exercises.prompt: Which principle does this design most clearly violate?
lines: private final Storage storage;     // only ever calls read()
// MemoryCache implements Storage; its backup() throws

options.why: Thumbnailer is forced to depend on `write` and `backup`, and implementers must fake them.
The throwing `backup` looks like LSP, but it is a symptom; the cause is the fat interface.
SRP is about a class's reasons to change; here a client is coupled to methods it never calls.
Depending on an interface is the right direction; the interface itself is too broad.

exercises.scenario: A `NotificationSender` interface declares `sendEmail`, `sendSms` and `sendPush`. The SMS vendor adapter throws for the other two, and the invoice job, which only sends email, needs three stubbed methods in every test.

options.why: Split into `EmailSender`, `SmsSender` and `PushSender`. Each adapter and client then depends only on its role.
Making adapters return silently would only hide the broken promise; the interface still forces it.
The adapter has a single job already; the shared interface is what is too wide.
The jobs already depend on an interface; its shape is the problem.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that asks for more than the class needs.
lines: interface Writer { void write(String key, String v); }
exercises.explanation: The constructor asks for a `ReadWriter` although `Report` only reads, so callers must supply write access and tests must fake it. Accept `Reader`.

exercises.prompt: Explain the Interface Segregation Principle in your own words, and how it relates to throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`.

modelAnswer.text: Clients should depend only on the methods they call, so interfaces are cut by client role rather than by implementer capability. A fat interface forces implementers to stub unsupported methods, usually by throwing UnsupportedOperationException, which is an LSP violation in disguise. Several small role interfaces fix both.

keyPoints: Cut interfaces by the client's role
Fat interfaces force stubs and wide mocks
Throwing stubs signal an ISP/LSP problem
A class may implement many role interfaces
